There's something uniquely reflective about a rainy commute. As droplets trace patterns on the window, the city transforms into a softer, quieter version of itself.

Moving into your first flat is an exciting milestone. It represents independence, growth, and the opportunity to create a space that truly reflects who you are.
Watching football

Watching football is an emotional rollercoaster. Every pass, tackle and goal brings fans together in a shared experience of hope, passion and excitement.
Wedding planning

Planning a wedding can be both thrilling and overwhelming. From selecting the perfect venue to curating the menu, every detail contributes to a day you'll treasure forever.
Going to the gym

Starting a gym routine is a powerful investment in your wellbeing. Consistency, patience, and a positive mindset are the keys to unlocking your fitness potential.
A new phone

Upgrading to a new phone offers exciting features and improved performance. It's a great opportunity to declutter, organise, and enhance your digital life.
Birthday at church

Celebrating a birthday with your church family is a beautiful reminder of community. Shared prayers and songs make the occasion meaningful and memorable.
Packing for holiday
Packed six outfits for a three day trip and forgot my charger. Classic me.
Packing for a holiday is all about balance. By planning outfits in advance and choosing versatile items, you can travel light while staying prepared for anything.
The post office queue
Lady in front of me was posting what I'm fairly sure was a whole goat leg to Lagos. Took 20 minutes.
Waiting in a post office queue offers an unexpected moment of pause in our busy lives, a chance to slow down, observe, and appreciate the rhythm of everyday life.
Learning to drive
My instructor said 'gently' so many times I started hearing it in my sleep. Passed on the third go.
Learning to drive is an empowering journey. With practice, patience, and the right guidance, new drivers build the confidence they need to navigate the road safely.
Christmas at home
Nobody agreed on the film so we watched the first 20 mins of three different ones and then argued about rice.
Christmas at home is a magical time filled with laughter, festive treats, and cherished traditions that remind us of the importance of family and togetherness.
Lost keys

Spent half an hour turning the house upside down looking for my keys. Found them in the fridge next to the milk. No idea how they got there, and my wife is never letting me forget it.
Bad haircut

The barber asked if I wanted the usual, and I said yes without thinking. Big mistake. I walked out looking about seventeen. I'll be wearing a cap until it grows back.
Gym membership

I went to the gym three times in January and kept paying until June. At this point it's basically a monthly donation to the fitness industry.
Slow wifi
Router's been dropping out every evening at 8, right when everyone's streaming. Rang the provider, was on hold 40 minutes, got told to switch it off and on. It worked. For one night.

The wifi keeps cutting out every evening around eight, just when everyone starts streaming. I called the provider, waited forty minutes, and was told to restart the router. It worked, but only for one night.
Birthday surprise

She said she didn't want a fuss, so naturally I organised a dinner for six, invited her sister and hid a cake in the car. All the 'no fuss' vanished the moment the cake appeared and she burst into tears.
Moving house
Packing was fine. Unpacking was the problem. Three weeks later there's still a box labelled 'misc' that nobody will admit to filling.
Packing was easy enough. Unpacking is the real challenge. Three weeks in, there is still a box marked 'misc' that nobody will admit to packing.
Church parking
Arrived 15 mins early to get a space. Still ended up three streets away behind a skip. Praise be for trainers, I suppose.
I arrived fifteen minutes early to secure a parking space and still ended up three streets away behind a skip. Thankfully I wore trainers.
Cooking jollof

First time cooking jollof for my in-laws. Kept stirring when I shouldn't have and the bottom caught. Mum-in-law ate two plates anyway and said the smoky bit was the best part. I'm not sure I believe her.

I cooked jollof rice for my in-laws for the first time. I stirred too much and the bottom caught. My mother-in-law had two plates and said the smoky part was the best bit. I'm not entirely sure she meant it.
Train delay
'Signal failure at Reading.' Always Reading. Sat in a carriage with a man eating a boiled egg for forty minutes. I now know more about that egg than I wanted to.
'Signal failure at Reading.' It's always Reading. I sat in a stuffy carriage for forty minutes next to a man eating a boiled egg, and I know far more about that egg than I ever wanted to.
New phone
Got the new phone, spent two hours moving my stuff across, and the only thing that didn't come with me was my alarm. Late for work by an hour. Thanks, technology.
I got a new phone and spent two hours transferring everything across. The only thing that didn't make the move was my alarm, so I was an hour late for work. Thanks, technology.
Garden
Planted tomatoes in May. By August I had one tomato and a lot of very healthy-looking weeds. The tomato was delicious though. Bit smug about it.
I planted tomatoes in May. By August I had exactly one tomato and a lot of very healthy weeds. The tomato was delicious, though, and I'm feeling rather smug about it.
Group chat
Family group chat has 47 unread messages and I'm scared to open it. Last time it was an argument about whose turn it was to host. For Christmas. In June.
The family group chat has forty-seven unread messages and I'm afraid to open it. Last time it was a debate over whose turn it was to host Christmas, and it was only June.
Walking at dusk

There is a stretch of the towpath where the lamps flicker on one by one, each a moment later than the last. I find myself walking more slowly there, in no hurry to arrive anywhere.
My grandmother's kitchen
Her kitchen smelled of onions and Dettol, and the radio was always half a station off. I never asked her why. Now I'd give a lot to hear the static.
My grandmother's kitchen smelled of onions and disinfectant, and her radio was never quite tuned to a station. I never asked why. Now I would give a great deal to hear that gentle static again.
Learning to drive at 40
The instructor said I braked like someone apologising to the road. He wasn't wrong. I passed on the second go, and I still say sorry at junctions.
My instructor said I braked like someone apologising to the road. He had a point. I passed on my second attempt, and I still murmur an apology at every junction.
The last bus home
The last bus is a small republic: the driver, three sleepers, a man guarding a kebab. Nobody speaks, and somehow we all agree on the rules.
The last bus home is a small republic of its own: a weary driver, a few sleepers, and a man guarding a kebab. Nobody speaks, yet everyone seems to agree on the rules.
Starting a business
Nobody tells you the hard part is the Tuesday after the launch, when the excitement has gone and the invoices haven't started. That's when you find out if you meant it.
Nobody warns you that the hardest part is the Tuesday after the launch, once the excitement fades and before the invoices arrive. That is when you learn whether you truly meant it.
Old photographs
In every photograph from that summer someone is looking at someone else, not at the camera. It took me thirty years to understand what the pictures were really of.
In every photograph from that summer, someone is looking at someone else rather than at the camera. It took me thirty years to understand what those pictures were really about.
First snow
The first snow always arrives overnight, so the morning has the feel of a secret: the same street, but quieter, and everyone's footprints still unwritten.
The first snow tends to arrive overnight, so the morning feels like a secret. It's the same street, only quieter, with no footprints yet written across it.
A hospital waiting room
Waiting rooms run on a currency of small kindnesses: a spare pen, a held door, a nod across the vending machine. Everyone is carrying something and pretending not to.
Hospital waiting rooms run on small kindnesses: a spare pen, a held door, a nod by the vending machine. Everyone is carrying something and quietly pretending they aren't.
Writing a eulogy
I wrote nine drafts. The tenth was just a list of things he used to say, and when I read it aloud, people laughed in the right places. That was the one.
I wrote nine drafts of the eulogy. The tenth was simply a list of the things he used to say, and when I read it aloud, people laughed in all the right places. That was the one.
Leaving a job

On my last day I was given a card signed by forty colleagues, and I realised I could recall the coffee orders of thirty. In a way, that was the whole job.
Sunday evenings
Sunday evenings have a particular light, the kind that makes the week ahead seem both close and negotiable. I iron shirts to give it somewhere to go.
Sunday evenings have a particular light, one that makes the week ahead feel both close and negotiable. I iron shirts, if only to give the feeling somewhere to go.
Teaching a child to ride
I let go of the saddle and didn't tell her. She rode ten metres before she noticed, and the look she gave me was half betrayal, half triumph. I've kept it.
I let go of the saddle without telling her. She rode ten metres before she noticed, and the look she gave me was half betrayal and half triumph. I have kept that look ever since.
